{"id": "23:99/q07", "question": "What does the dying person see or undergo that prompts the plea?", "turns_on": "The notes describe different experiences at death: exposure of neglected acts, sight of the Fire, or confusion under assault.", "positions": [{"id": "23:99/q07/p1", "position": "He recognizes neglected deeds, withheld rights, disobedience, or the truth of the afterlife.", "reasons": "Muqatil says the Angel of Death reveals sins and shame; al-Suddi says few good deeds and many bad deeds. A prophetic report through a man of Banu Haritha says impediments to obligations appear before or between his eyes; Razi's prophetic report says withheld rights appear; Jabir's report says obstacles to truth gather before his eyes. Tabari and Kashshaf stress remorse over neglected obedience, faith and good works. Baydawi, Qushayri, Bursevi and Kuranyolu likewise describe regret once truth or the afterlife is visible. Qurtubi cites 8:50 for soul-taking angels. Al-Qushayri, through Abu Hayyan, says denial persisted despite proofs until certainty and angels arrived."}, {"id": "23:99/q07/p2", "position": "He sees his allotted place in the Fire and asks to repent.", "reasons": "Abu Hurayra's report, transmitted by Ibn Kathir and al-Durr, says a dead unbeliever sees his seat in the Fire, is told his lifespan is over, and then suffers constriction and creatures in the grave. Al-Hasan says the Fire becomes clear to one without God's friendship."}, {"id": "23:99/q07/p3", "position": "Devils and punishment guards bewilder him into a habitual appeal to created beings.", "reasons": "Al-Suhayli, reported by Burhan and Itqan, says the person speaks incoherently under their assault; Burhan calls the appeal a worldly habit."}]}
{"id": "23:99/q08", "question": "Is the dying request spoken aloud?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:99/q08/p1", "position": "It may be inward or inaudible to people nearby.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan says even a mute person asks and bystanders do not hear; al-Suddi says descendants do not hear. Nahhas points to speech within oneself in 58:8; Qurtubi applies the same verse to the request."}]}
{"id": "23:99/q09", "question": "Where does the speaker ask to return?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:99/q09/p1", "position": "To worldly life.", "reasons": "Tabari, Ibn Abbas as reported by Wahidi, Wahidi's Wajiz, Thalabi, Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and others explicitly name the world. Damghani gives rajaʿa the sense 'send back or return,' grouping this plea with 20:40 and 67:4. Ibn Kathir says return would allow repair of ruined deeds. Biqai calls the world the abode of knowledge."}]}
{"id": "23:99/q10", "question": "What does the speaker hope to do if returned?", "turns_on": "Whether the sought good is left general, specified as faith or its testimony, or exemplified by neglected financial and pilgrimage duties.", "positions": [{"id": "23:99/q10/p1", "position": "Do the righteous work neglected, especially faith and obedience, rather than resume worldly ties.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Kashshaf specify neglected faith; Tabari, Thalabi, Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and the prophetic reports specify good works or withheld duties. Qatada says it is obedience, not family or tribe. Ikrima and Ibn Abbas identify the wished-for good as saying 'There is no god but God.' Samarrai says this verse asks for righteousness generally rather than charity specifically, since salvation here is framed outside a wealth passage. Study Quran compares pleas for charity or righteousness in 63:10, 32:12, 2:167, 26:102, 35:37 and 39:58. The general and specific formulations are compatible descriptions of the intended good."}, {"id": "23:99/q10/p2", "position": "Complete withheld alms and pilgrimage.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says one who neglected charity and pilgrimage seeks return, citing 63:10; al-Awza'i narrows it to withheld alms. This is a specific instance of repairing neglected obligations, but its proponents use it to broaden the asker beyond unbelievers."}]}
{"id": "23:99/q11", "question": "Why is 'return me' phrased as a plural command?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural is conventional reverence, a change to angelic addressees, repetition, self-magnification, combined address, or confused speech; Ibn Malik disputes the permissibility of plural prayer to God.", "positions": [{"id": "23:99/q11/p1", "position": "The singular God is addressed with an honorific plural.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba compares royal 'we' and scriptural usage (12:3, 54:49); the Kufan grammarian cites 19:9; Nahhas, Wahidi's grammarians (50:43), Zajjaj, Thalabi, Baghawi, Kashshaf, Razi, Nasafi and others invoke Arabic reverence or divine plural forms. Samīn prefers this and cites poetry against Ibn Malik's prayer restriction; he notes scriptural plurals. Bursevi rejects the claim this usage is only late Arabic. Ibn Ashur says masculine plural can honor even a woman, citing al-Arji's siwakum and Ja'far's ba'dakum. Asad says most commentators favor it. Baydawi, Qurtubi, Biqai and Ibn Atiyya also offer it. Alusi says poetry confirms it and explains one honored person as treated like a group."}, {"id": "23:99/q11/p2", "position": "He first invokes God, then addresses the soul-taking or punishment angels in the plural.", "reasons": "Tabari and Ibn Jurayj describe a shift of addressee. Al-Mubarrad prefers it and cites al-Ahwas and al-Nabigha shifting from a house to its owner. Razi says 'Lord' can be an oath by God's right; Samīn and Alusi posit an omitted 'angels of my Lord,' with Samīn citing pronoun shift in 7:4. Burhan treats رب as a cry for help. The same reading appears in Thalabi, Wahidi, Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Itqan and Study Quran."}, {"id": "23:99/q11/p3", "position": "The plural expresses repeated pleading: 'return me, return me, return me.'", "reasons": "Al-Mazini, Nahhas and Qurtubi compare 50:24, 'throw him,' understood as repeated throwing; Abu al-Baqa also invokes the dual command and qifa nabki. Baydawi offers repetition; Asad reports Baydawi arguing from pre-Islamic poetry and reflects it by repeating the plea. Alusi compares qifa nabki but al-Khafaji objects that singular imperative has no plural pronoun; al-Khafaji instead proposes swapping word forms regardless of meaning. Alusi rejects this as excessive, suggesting honorific group address can make the action resemble repeated group action; he leaves open whether dual address can similarly honor one."}, {"id": "23:99/q11/p4", "position": "The speaker addresses himself in the plural to magnify himself.", "reasons": "Burhan reports this minority explanation: ارجعون means singular ارجعني, with the speaker's self-aggrandizing 'we.'"}, {"id": "23:99/q11/p5", "position": "The plural addresses God and the angels together.", "reasons": "Biqai offers this among alternatives while describing the angels of punishment at death."}, {"id": "23:99/q11/p6", "position": "A plural prayer form to God is impermissible because it suggests plurality in Him.", "reasons": "Ibn Malik says he knows no one allowing a supplicant to say يا رحيمون. Samīn rejects the restriction with scriptural plural forms used for reverence."}, {"id": "23:99/q11/p7", "position": "Confusion under devils and punishment guards produces an incoherent habitual appeal.", "reasons": "Al-Suhayli, reported in Burhan and Itqan, regards the utterance as a confused appeal of the kind the person addressed to created beings in life."}]}
{"id": "23:99/q12", "question": "How are the adjacent hamzas in 'came one' recited?", "turns_on": "Treatment of two adjacent open hamzas, including which hamza Abu Amr elides and the resulting madd relation.", "positions": [{"id": "23:99/q12/p1", "position": "Both hamzas are fully pronounced.", "reasons": "Ibn Amir, Asim, Hamza, al-Kisai, Khalaf and Rawh fully pronounce them in all five relevant classes; Ibn Mihran alone reports easing for Rawh. Al-Tadhkira, al-Taysir, al-Kafi, al-Shatibiyya, Talkhis al-Ibarat and al-Tajrid transmit both full pronunciation and easing. Ibn al-Jazari classifies جاء أحدهم among 16 two-fatha forms in 29 places."}, {"id": "23:99/q12/p2", "position": "The adjacent hamzas are eased rather than both fully pronounced.", "reasons": "Makki, al-Mahdawi, Ibn Sufyan and al-Unwan choose easing; al-Rawda, al-Mubhij, both al-Ghayas and Talkhis also transmit it. Al-Tajrid's author says he read it from al-Farisi and Abd al-Baqi; multiple manuals also give both options. Ibn Shurayh's particular easing like waw is rejected by Ibn al-Jazari because it would require impermissible conversion or rounding of the hamza's kasra."}, {"id": "23:99/q12/p3", "position": "Abu Amr drops the first hamza.", "reasons": "Most performance authorities say so and Ibn al-Jazari chooses it by analogy with like letters; which hamza drops determines whether the preceding madd is connected or separate."}, {"id": "23:99/q12/p4", "position": "Abu Amr drops the second hamza.", "reasons": "Ibn Ghalbun and al-Hammami report this, following al-Khalil and grammarians; the position changes whether the preceding madd is connected or separate."}]}
{"id": "23:99/q13", "question": "What other hamza and madd rules are cited alongside this reading?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:99/q13/p1", "position": "A second like hamza changed to a madd letter lengthens before a consonant, but otherwise has ordinary madd length.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari says the longer duration resolves two adjacent sukuns. For جاء آل لوط and جاء آل فرعون, al-Dani reports disagreement between replacement and easing because an alif follows; some reject replacement to avoid consecutive alifs. These are related examples, not variant wording of this verse."}]}

{"id": "23:99/q16", "question": "What reports contrast a believer's response to death with this plea?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:99/q16/p1", "position": "A believer offered return declines the world's sorrow and chooses to go forward to God; the unbeliever asks to return.", "reasons": "Thalabi reports the Prophet speaking to Aisha; Ibn Atiyya and al-Durr transmit comparable reports. {"id": "23:99/q17", "question": "What happens in Abu Hurayra's report about the dead unbeliever?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:99/q17/p1", "position": "He sees his seat in the Fire, requests return and repentance, is refused, and suffers in the grave.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir and al-Durr transmit Abu Hurayra: his allotted lifespan is said to be over; the grave constricts and its creatures torment him."}]}
{"id": "23:99/q18", "question": "What response and practical warning accompany the plea?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:99/q18/p1", "position": "The request is refused; people should act and turn to God while return is still possible.", "reasons": "Thalabi says the following كلا rebukes and refuses; Muhammad ibn Ka'b depicts God answering that it is only a word. Ibn Kathir says return is refused at death and repeatedly at resurrection, judgment and sight of the Fire, citing 63:10–11, 14:44, 7:53, 32:12, 6:27–28, 42:44, 40:11–12 and 35:37. Al-Qushayri says the distressed submit when escape ends and are told to have done so earlier; he reports a poem urging the soul to return before the road is blocked. Abu Uthman's inward counsel urges obedience, avoiding spiritual claims and correcting practice. Qatada transmits al-Ala ibn Ziyad's exercise of imagining a granted reprieve and says the living should perform the obedience the unbeliever wished to perform. Biqai warns that devils are most dangerous at death, when the veil lifts, and urges striving and prayer for protection. Study Quran describes the conclusion as warning disbelievers that their wish comes too late."}]}
{"id": "23:99/q19", "question": "Can the dead return to worldly life after this plea?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:99/q19/p1", "position": "No return to worldly life is granted after death, though resurrection will occur.", "reasons": "Jishumi explicitly opposes the Imamis and affirms resurrection. {"id": "23:99/q20", "question": "What does the requested return imply about human action?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:99/q20/p1", "position": "People own their deeds and ability, so the plea to return for good work rebuts compulsion.", "reasons": "Jishumi argues the promise to do good on return would be meaningless if human deeds and capacity were not their own."}]}
{"id": "23:99/q21", "question": "What does the request show about knowledge of one's fate before death?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:99/q21/p1", "position": "Before death people know with certainty whether they belong to God's allies or enemies.", "reasons": "Qurtubi infers this from the request itself: without such certainty, they would not seek return."}]}
{"id": "23:99/q22", "question": "Why ask for return if it is known to be impossible?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:99/q22/p1", "position": "A person may permissibly supplicate for the impossible, or merely express hope and grief.", "reasons": "Razi says knowledge that return cannot happen does not prevent such supplication; Kuranyolu reports Razi that the dying person knows return is impossible yet grieves at dying unbelieving."}]}

{"id": "24:27/q05", "question": "What does tastaʾnisū require or mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb names formal permission, the investigation before it, the signal announcing arrival, the ease resulting from consent, or greeting itself; reports, Arabic usage, morphology, and context are cited.", "positions": [{"id": "24:27/q05/p1", "position": "Ask permission to enter, seeking the household's welcome and consent.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Qatāda, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mālik and many commentators gloss it with istiʾdhān.
